title: flow_grpo
specification: Flow-GRPO integrates online RL into flow matching models for text-to-image generation. To accelerate training, we apply a Denoising Reduction strategy: during online data collection, we set the number of denoising steps to T=10, while retaining the original T=40 for inference. A group of images is sampled with this reduced schedule, and rewards are computed from the final denoised outputs. The GRPO objective is then maximized by averaging over the T=10 denoising steps the clipped policy ratio times the normalized advantage, along with a KL regularization term against a reference model. This design enables efficient RL training without sacrificing image quality at test time.
blocker: Without this clarification, implementers would not know whether to train on all or a subset of denoising steps, and could experience numerical instability from including the last step or waste computation on unnecessary steps.
clarification: How many of the reduced denoising steps are actually used during training? Is the final step excluded, and what is the rationale?
evidence: Author clarification on the timestep_fraction parameter and step exclusion rationale.
reference: Flow-GRPO improves flow matching text-to-image models via online RL. It converts the deterministic ODE to an SDE for stochastic sampling and applies Denoising Reduction to speed up training. During training, a group of images is generated per prompt using a reduced number of denoising steps T (e.g., 10). Critically, only the first floor(T * timestep_fraction) denoising steps are used for policy optimization; the final step closest to the clean image is excluded to avoid numerical overflow from a very small sigma. With the default timestep_fraction=0.99 and T=10, training uses the first 9 steps. The GRPO loss is computed over these selected steps, incorporating a clipped advantage and a KL penalty against the reference model. Inference still uses the full T=40 steps, ensuring high-quality outputs. This clarifies that the denoising reduction accelerates training not only by reducing total steps but by further restricting which steps are optimized, preventing numerical issues while maintaining performance.

title: Time-MoE
specification: We evaluate TIME-MoE on six long-term forecasting benchmarks: ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, and Global Temperature. For zero-shot forecasting, the pre-trained model is applied directly to the test set without any fine-tuning. Input lengths are {512, 1024, 2048, 3072} and prediction horizons are {96, 192, 336, 720}. For in-distribution (full-shot) forecasting, we fine-tune the pre-trained TIME-MoE models on the train split of the above-mentioned six benchmarks and set the number of finetuning epochs to only one. Performance is measured by mean square error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE).
blocker: Without explicitly defining zero-shot vs. full-shot evaluation paths and data scaling procedure for GlobalTemp, one cannot reproduce the exact numbers reported in the paper for this dataset.
clarification: How are zero-shot and full-shot evaluations conducted for the GlobalTemp dataset, including any data normalization steps?
evidence: Details on whether the test set is scaled using training set statistics and whether fine-tuning uses the scaled training data, plus the exact zero-shot and full-shot evaluation flow.
reference: TIME-MoE is a decoder-only time series foundation model that uses a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture for universal forecasting. The model is evaluated on six long-term forecasting benchmarks, including Global Temperature. For the Global Temperature dataset, the first 1000 dimensions are selected. For each dimension, a ZeroScaler is trained using the training set (computing the mean and standard deviation) and then applied to both the training and test sets. In the zero-shot evaluation, the pre-trained TIME-MoE model is applied directly to the scaled test set to generate predictions. In the full-shot evaluation, the pre-trained model is first fine-tuned for one epoch on the scaled training data, and then the fine-tuned model is evaluated on the scaled test set. All 1000 dimensions are used for metric calculation. Input lengths are set to {512, 1024, 2048, 3072} and prediction horizons to {96, 192, 336, 720}. Performance is measured by mean square error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE).

title: Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Neural Networks
specification: We consider link prediction on several hierarchical graph datasets, including Disease and Disease-M.  As a Euclidean baseline we implement a simple Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP).  The MLP consists of two fully connected layers with ReLU activations, taking the Euclidean node features as input and outputting node embeddings.  For link prediction, the embeddings of two nodes are combined using the Fermi-Dirac decoder to produce a probability score for the edge.  The model is trained with binary cross-entropy loss and the Adam optimizer.  This baseline allows us to measure the benefit of the graph structure and hyperbolic geometry compared to a purely feature-based Euclidean approach.
blocker: The undocumented normalization artificially restricts the Euclidean feature space, causing the baseline to perform far worse than it should. Correcting this reveals that the Euclidean MLP can match or exceed hyperbolic models on tasks previously claimed to require hyperbolicity.
clarification: Is the input feature normalization to the unit ball intended to be part of the Euclidean MLP baseline, or should the features be used as-is?
evidence: Check the original code implementation in the public repository to see if normalization is present and whether it represents the authors' intended behavior.
reference: The goal is to compare hyperbolic graph neural networks with a simple Euclidean MLP baseline on link prediction tasks using hierarchical graph datasets (Disease, Disease-M, Airport).  The input consists of Euclidean node features.  The MLP baseline transforms these features through two fully connected layers with ReLU activations, producing node embeddings.  For link prediction, the embeddings of a node pair are combined with the Fermi-Dirac decoder to obtain an edge probability.  The model is trained with binary cross-entropy loss using the Adam optimizer.  Evaluation is performed with ROC AUC, reporting mean and standard deviation over 5 trials.  For the Euclidean MLP baseline, do not apply any normalization that would constrain the features to the unit ball; the features should be used as-is.  To ensure numerical stability when computing the Fermi-Dirac decoder probability, clamp the exponential argument to a maximum of 20:  `probs = 1. / (torch.exp(((dist - self.r) / self.t).clamp_max(20)) + 1.0)`

title: Discover-then-Name: Task-Agnostic Concept Bottlenecks via Automated Concept Discovery
specification: DN‑CBM discovers concepts by training a sparse autoencoder on frozen CLIP features with an L1 sparsity penalty and dead‑neuron resampling every 10 epochs. After discovery, each concept direction is compared via similarity to CLIP text embeddings of a large vocabulary, and the top word is assigned as the name. For downstream classification, concept strengths are extracted and a linear probe (no bias, L1‑regularized) is trained with cross‑entropy loss. Evaluation covers top‑1 accuracy on standard test sets and includes interventions where specific concept strengths are zeroed. The method uses no data augmentation and pre‑computes features for speed.
blocker: The choice of similarity function—e.g., cosine vs. dot product—directly affects which word gets assigned to each concept direction, especially if embeddings are not unit‑normalized; without specifying, the naming procedure is ambiguous and can lead to different concept sets.
clarification: What exact similarity metric is used to compare concept directions with text embeddings during naming?
evidence: Find the exact algorithm detail in the original paper.
reference: The method, Discover-then-Name Concept Bottleneck Model (DN-CBM), is an automated concept-bottleneck pipeline for image classification. Given a frozen CLIP feature extractor and an unlabeled image caption dataset (e.g., CC3M), it proceeds in three phases. (1) Concept Discovery: a sparse autoencoder (SAE) is trained on CLIP embeddings of the unlabeled images, producing an overcomplete latent code. The encoder maps an embedding to a sparse vector of concept strengths; the decoder reconstructs the embedding and its columns serve as prototype concept directions. Training minimizes a combined reconstruction error (MSE) and L1 sparsity penalty on the latent activations. (2) Naming: each concept direction is compared via cosine similarity to CLIP text embeddings of a large vocabulary, and the top word is assigned as the concept name. (3) Bottleneck Construction and Classification: For any downstream image classification task, the SAE encoder and CLIP backbone are frozen, and concept strengths are extracted as the latent vectors. A linear probe (without bias) is fitted on these concept strengths to predict class labels, using cross-entropy loss with an L1 penalty on the linear weights to promote sparse explanations. Evaluation measures top-1 classification accuracy on held-out test sets (ImageNet, Places365, CIFAR-10/100) against baselines (Linear Probe, Zero-Shot CLIP, LF-CBM, LaBo, CDM, DCLIP). Concept-based interventions are performed by zeroing the strengths of selected concepts.

title: GANSpace: Discovering Interpretable GAN Controls
specification: GANSpace discovers interpretable latent directions in pretrained GANs. For StyleGAN, N z are sampled, mapped to w, PCA on w yields V. For BigGAN, N z are sampled and forward-propagated to an intermediate layer to obtain feature tensors; PCA yields basis V and mean, then least-squares regression yields latent basis U. Editing: latent codes perturbed by linear combinations of V or U. Layer-wise editing applied to specific layer ranges. Slider interface. Qualitative evaluation on FFHQ, Cars, Cats, ImageNet datasets, comparing to random directions and supervised baselines.
blocker: The choice of layer greatly affects the semantic content of the PCA basis; without knowing the exact layer, implementers may select a suboptimal one and fail to obtain interpretable or useful directions.
clarification: At which specific layer of BigGAN should the feature tensors be extracted for PCA?
evidence: Find the exact preprocessing detail in the original paper.
reference: GANSpace is an unsupervised method for discovering interpretable latent directions in pretrained Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and applying them for layer-wise image synthesis control. The method operates on existing StyleGAN or BigGAN generators without retraining. It proceeds in two main stages: (1) Principal component analysis (PCA) basis discovery: For StyleGAN, N random latent vectors z are sampled and mapped through the mapping network M to obtain w vectors; PCA is computed on these w vectors to get a basis V. For BigGAN, N random z are sampled and forward-propagated to a chosen intermediate layer (the first linear layer) to obtain feature tensors; PCA is computed on these tensors to get a basis V and mean μ, then the basis is transferred to latent space by solving a least-squares regression from PCA coordinates x back to z, yielding a latent basis U. (2) Editing: An image is generated from a latent code; the code is perturbed by adding a linear combination of the basis vectors (V for StyleGAN, U for BigGAN) multiplied by user-controlled coefficients. To achieve layer-wise editing, for StyleGAN, the perturbation is applied only to the w inputs of a specified layer range; for BigGAN, the intermediate Skip-z inputs can be varied independently per layer, analogous to style mixing. The discovered directions are explored interactively via a slider-based interface. Evaluations are conducted qualitatively on pretrained models trained on datasets including FFHQ, Cars, Cats, and ImageNet, comparing edits to random directions and supervised baselines.
